title: Aerosol Properties, Aerosol-Cryosphere & Aerosol–Cloud–Radiation Interaction
text:
Understanding the Black Carbon dynamics and Black Carbon-Cryosphere Interactions in the Hindu Kush Himalayan Region



The Himalayas are often called the “Third Pole” because they hold more ice than anywhere else on Earth outside the Arctic and Antarctic. Nearly two billion people depend on the rivers that flow from these mountains. My research focuses on a simple but powerful question:


How is air pollution—especially black carbon—changing the future of Himalayan snow and glaciers?


To answer this, I work across the Hindu Kush Himalayan (HKH) region, and my research focuses on understanding how black carbon (BC) and other light‑absorbing aerosols influence this region, one of the world’s most climate‑sensitive mountain systems. Through a combination of high‑altitude fieldwork, ground-based observations, chemical transport modeling, remote sensing, and radiative transfer simulations, my work quantifies how aerosols are transported, how they modify atmospheric and surface energy budgets, and how they accelerate snow and glacier melt.



What is black carbon, and why does it matter?


Black carbon (BC) is a tiny particle released when we burn things—diesel, firewood, crop residue, forest biomass. It’s dark, so it absorbs sunlight extremely well. When BC lands on snow or ice, it darkens the surface, accelerating melting.
Think of it like wearing a black T‑shirt on a sunny day—you feel warmer. Glaciers feel the same effect.



Black Carbon in the Central Himalaya: Concentrations, Sources, and Cryospheric Impacts



High-altitude BC observations near Yala Glacier


At 4900 m a.s.l., near the Yala Glacier, one of the highest BC monitoring efforts in the HKH. Year-long measurements revealed:

Peak atmospheric BC concentrations during pre-monsoon (up to 0.73 μg m⁻³)
BC in surface snow ranging from 96–542 ng g⁻¹, sufficient to measurably darken the glacier surface
Surface albedo reduction of 0.8–3.8%, simulated using the SNICAR model
BC-induced glacier mass loss contributes ~39% of the total melt during the pre-monsoon

These findings highlight the disproportionate sensitivity of Himalayan glaciers to even small amounts of deposited BC.


Source attribution


Using both in situ absorption Ångström exponent (AAE) analysis and WRF-Chem tagged tracer simulations, we quantified BC origins:

~44% from biomass burning (in situ AAE)
~77% from anthropogenic sources (model-based)
Major regional contributors: Nepal + India, followed by China

This dual-method approach provided one of the most robust BC source assessments for a Himalayan glacier environment.




Regional BC Variability Across the Hindu Kush Himalaya



To address the severe observational gap in the central Himalaya, nine long-term BC monitoring stations were establihsed across Nepal, Bhutan, and the Tibetan Plateau (102–4920 m a.s.l.). Analysis of 2016–2019 data revealed:


Extreme spatial heterogeneity



Annual mean BC ranged from 36 ng m⁻³ (high-altitude) to 45,737 ng m⁻³ (urban/lowland)
High-altitude sites peaked in pre-monsoon, while low-altitude sites peaked in winter



Dominance of biomass burning


Across most sites, biomass burning contributed >50% of BC, except in Kathmandu, where fossil fuel sources were more prominent.


Long-range transport pathways


Using concentration-weighted trajectories (CWT) and frequency analysis, we found:

Wintertime pollution is strongly influenced by westerly long-range transport
Monsoon brings South Asian emissions deep into the mountains
Valley dynamics amplify pollution in mid-altitude basins

This work provides the most comprehensive BC climatology for the HKH region to date.




Aerosol Composition, Radiative Forcing, and Atmospheric Heating in the Central Himalaya



Using AERONET, CALIPSO, and radiative transfer modeling, I quantified the contributions of BC, organic carbon (OC/BrC), and dust to aerosol absorption and atmospheric heating across nine stations (110–4901 m a.s.l.).


Key findings



BC dominates absorption (>50%) at most mid- and high-altitude sites
Dust influence increases toward low-altitude Indo-Gangetic Plain sites
CALIPSO profiles show significant aerosol loading above 3 km, with carbonaceous aerosols present even above 5 km
Radiative forcing increases toward lower altitudes but remains substantial at high elevations
Vertical heating rates reveal strong atmospheric warming, critical for glacier mass balance and monsoon dynamics

This work improves the representation of aerosol–radiation interactions in climate models and highlights the vulnerability of Himalayan glaciers to elevated aerosol layers.







Overall Contribution



Across these studies, my research provides:

High-elevation BC observations in one of the world’s most remote cryospheric environments
Quantitative attribution of BC sources using both observational and modeling approaches
Evidence of BC-driven glacier melt, including one of the first estimates of its fractional contribution (~39%)
A regional-scale assessment of BC variability across the HKH
Aerosol composition and radiative forcing estimates essential for climate modeling

Together, these works advance our understanding of how aerosols shape the climate and cryosphere of the Himalaya—informing mitigation strategies, regional policy, and future climate projections.




Why this research matters



The Himalaya is warming faster than the global average. Understanding how pollution accelerates glacier melt is essential for:

Water security for millions of people
Disaster risk reduction (floods, landslides, glacial lake outbursts)
Climate policy in South Asia
Protecting fragile mountain ecosystems

My work helps identify which pollutants, from which regions, and during which seasons have the biggest impact—so that governments and communities can take targeted action.




Priority Policy Actions





Accelerate clean household energy transitions



Replace biomass cookstoves with clean alternatives in rural and mountain communities.



Regulate and modernize brick kilns and small industries



Adopt cleaner kiln technologies and enforce emissions standards.



Reduce agricultural residue burning



Promote mechanized alternatives, incentives, and community‑level enforcement.



Strengthen forest fire management



Invest in early detection, rapid response, and community fire‑prevention programs.



Expand high‑altitude monitoring networks



Support long‑term BC and aerosol monitoring to guide policy and track progress.



Build a regional BC mitigation framework



Facilitate cooperation among Nepal, India, Bhutan, China, and Pakistan on emissions reduction and data sharing.

title: Aerosol composition, transport, and radiative impact derived from ground-based and satellite remote sensing in the Central Himalaya
text: The study aims to quantify the individual contributions of light-absorbing aerosols, i.e., BC, OC, and dust, to the aerosol absorption over the Central Himalaya, a poorly studied and sensitive region, ranging from low to high altitude, using the in-situ observations. The seasonal mean SSA, AAOD, and AOD values were found in the range of 0.76 ± 0.017 to 0.99 ± 0.005, 0.001 ± 0.0004 to 0.067 ± 0.034, and 0.083 ± 0.003 to 0.751 ± 0.328 at all sites. Several stations showed lower SSA values during the pre-monsoon, inferring the dominance of the light-absorbing aerosols originating from natural and anthropogenic sources. We utilized external and internal mixing approaches to estimate aerosol component fractions. The results from the external mixing approach showed the presence of >50 % of BC and < 10 % of the dust in most of the high and mid-altitude sites. However, the presence of dust was greater at the low-altitude sites. Nevertheless, the presence of dust was estimated in almost all the sites, considering the internal mixing case. The results from both approaches agreed well with the CALIPSO aerosol subtype. Though a few discrepancies were found, the MG approximation occasionally overestimated the dust fraction. The aerosol radiative forcing at the surface and in the atmosphere showed an increasing trend toward the lower altitude, except for a few anomalies at Kathmandu and Lumbini. The vertical aerosol extinction profiles were also analyzed, and vertical heating rates were calculated, which revealed a significant loading of aerosols above the 3 km altitude and a substantial presence of carbonaceous aerosols and heating over the 5 km altitude, crucial for the survival of glaciers. The study will improve the regional representation of aerosol compositions in climate simulations, the quantification of impact on the glaciers, and aerosol-induced changes in the hydrological cycle in the region.

title: Simulation of Meteorological Conditions Using a High-resolution Model Case Study: Chamoli Rock-Ice Avalanche Event (Uttarakhand, India)
text: The present study aims to analyze the high-resolution model-simulated meteorological conditions during the Chamoli rock-ice avalanche event, which occurred on 7 February 2021 in the Chamoli district of Uttarakhand, India. Recent changes in climate of the high-altitude Himalayan region have resulted in the formation of numerous water bodies ranging from meltwater ponds to new lakes on the surface of glaciers, while the existing ones are expanding dramatically. The Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model is used to simulate the spatiotemporal distribution of meteorological variables pre- and post-event. The numerical simulations are carried out over two fine resolution nested model domains covering the Uttarakhand region over a period of 2 weeks (2 February to 13 February 2021). The model-simulated meteorological variables, e.g., air temperature, surface temperature, turbulent heat flux, radiative fluxes, heat and momentum transfer coefficients, specific humidity and upper wind patterns, were found to show significant departures from their usual patterns starting from 72 h until a few hours before the rock-ice avalanche event. The average 2 m air and surface temperatures near the avalanche site during the 48 h before the event were found to be much lower than the average temperatures post-event. This research provides valuable insights into the atmospheric dynamics preceding the event that could potentially be the precursors for the event. This study highlighted the critical role of temperature and precipitation, together with turbulent and radiative fluxes as well as wind speed, in rock-ice avalanche initiation and suggested that the unusual temperature fluctuations, coupled with intense wind and precipitation, could be the primary precursors for the rock-ice avalanche event. In-situ observations and the ERA5-Land dataset also confirm these findings. The total turbulent heat flux mostly remained downward (negative) in the 72 h before the event and was found to have an exceptionally large negative value a few hours before the rock-ice avalanche event. The model-simulated rainfall and Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM, IMERG)-derived rainfall suggest that the part of the Himalayan region falling in the simulation domain received a significant amount of rainfall on 4 February, around 48 h prior to the event, while the rest of the days pre- and post-event were mostly dry.. This study explicitly presents out the meteorological conditions that prevailed during, before, and after the rock-ice avalanche event to better understand the weather conditions as a possible triggering factor. Our results may be helpful in further studies to find the possible trigger mechanisms of the event with regards to the freezing and thawing of rock masses.

title: Variability of ambient black carbon concentration in the Central Himalaya and its assessment over the Hindu Kush Himalayan region
text: During 2015–2018, eight black carbon (BC) monitoring sites were established in Nepal and Bhutan to fill a significant data gap regarding BC measurement in Central Himalaya. This manuscript analyzes and presents data from these eight stations and one additional station on the Tibetan plateau (TP). Complex topography, varied emission sources, and atmospheric transport pathways significantly impacted the BC concentrations across these stations, with annual mean concentrations varying from 36 ng m−3 to 45,737 ng m−3. Higher annual mean concentrations (5609 ± 4515 ng m−3) were recorded at low-altitude sites than in other locations, with seasonal concentrations highest in the winter (7316 ± 2541 ng m−3). In contrast, the annual mean concentrations were lowest at high-altitude sites (376 ± 448 ng m−3); the BC concentrations at these sites peaked during the pre-monsoon season (930 ± 685 ng m−3). Potential source contributions to the total observed BC were analyzed using the absorption angstrom exponent (AAE). AAE analysis showed the dominance of biomass burning sources (>50 %), except in Kathmandu. By combining our data with previously published literature, we put our measurements in perspective by presenting a comprehensive assessment of BC concentrations and their variability over the Hindu Kush Himalayan (HKH) region. The BC levels in all three geographic regions, high, mid, and low altitude significantly influenced by the persistent seasonal meteorology. However, the mid-altitude stations were substantially affected by valley dynamics and urbanization. The low-altitude stations experienced high BC concentrations during the winter and post-monsoon seasons. Concentration weighted trajectory (CWT) and frequency analyses revealed the dominance of long-range transported pollution during winter over HKH, from west to east. South Asian sources remained significant during the monsoon season. During pre- and post-monsoon, the local, regional, and long-distance pollution varied depending on the location of the receptor site.

title: Learnings from COVID-19 Forced Lockdown on Regional Air Quality and Mitigation Potential for South Asia
text: South Asia is a hotspot of air pollution with limited resilience and hence, understanding the mitigation potential of different sources is critically important. In this context the country lockdown initiated to combat the COVID-19 pandemic (during March and April 2020 that is the pre-monsoon season) provides an unique opportunity for studying the relative impacts of different emission sources in the region. Here, we analyze changes in levels of air quality species across the region during selected lockdown periods using satellite and in-situ datasets. This analysis compares air quality levels during the lockdown against pre-lockdown conditions as well as against regional long-term mean. Satellite derived AOD, NO2, and CO data indicates an increase of 9.5%, 2%, and 2.6%, respectively, during the 2020 lockdown period compared to pre-lockdown over the South Asia domain. However, individual country statistics, urban site data, and industrial grid analysis within the region indicate a more varied picture. Cities with high traffic loads reported a reduction of 12–39% in columnar NO2 during lockdown, in-situ PM2.5 measurements indicate a 23–56% percent reduction over the country capitals and columnar SO2 has an approximate reduction of 50% over industrial areas. In contrast, pollutant emissions from natural sources e.g., from biomass burning were observed to be adversely affecting the air quality in this period potentially masking expected lockdown related air quality improvements. This study demonstrates the need for a more nuanced and situation specific understanding of sources of air pollutants (anthropogenic and natural) and for these sources to be better understood from the local to the regional scale. Without this deeper understanding, mitigation strategies cannot be effectively targeted, wasting limited resources as well as risking unintended consequences both for the atmosphere and how mitigation action is perceived by the wider public.

title: 7 February Chamoli (Uttarakhand, India) Rock-Ice Avalanche Disaster: Model-Simulated Prevailing Meteorological Conditions
text: The present study aims to analyze the high-resolution model-simulated meteorological conditions during the Chamoli rock-ice avalanche event, which occurred on 7 February 2021 in the Chamoli district of Uttarakhand, India (30.37° N, 79.73° E). The Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model is used to simulate the spatiotemporal distribution of meteorological variables pre- and post-event. The numerical simulations are carried out over two fine resolution nested model domains covering the Uttarakhand region over a period of 2 weeks (2 February to 13 February 2021). The model-simulated meteorological variables, e.g., air temperature, surface temperature, turbulent heat flux, radiative fluxes, heat and momentum transfer coefficients, specific humidity and upper wind patterns, were found to show significant departures from their usual patterns starting from 72 h until a few hours before the rock-ice avalanche event. The average 2 m air and surface temperatures near the avalanche site during the 48 h before the event were found to be much lower than the average temperatures post-event. In-situ observations and the ERA5-Land dataset also confirm these findings. The total turbulent heat flux mostly remained downward (negative) in the 72 h before the event and was found to have an exceptionally large negative value a few hours before the rock-ice avalanche event. The model-simulated rainfall and Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM, IMERG)-derived rainfall suggest that the part of the Himalayan region falling in the simulation domain received a significant amount of rainfall on 4 February, around 48 h prior to the event, while the rest of the days pre- and post-event were mostly dry. The results presented here might be helpful in further studies to identify the possible trigger factors of this event.

title: A case study using 2019 pre-monsoon snow and stream chemistry in the Khumbu region, Nepal
text: This case study provides a framework for future monitoring and evidence for human source pollution in the Khumbu region, Nepal. We analyzed the chemical composition (major ions, major/trace elements, black carbon, and stable water isotopes) of pre-monsoon stream water (4300–5250 m) and snow (5200–6665 m) samples collected from Mt. Everest, Mt. Lobuche, and the Imja Valley during the 2019 pre-monsoon season, in addition to a shallow ice core recovered from the Khumbu Glacier (5300 m). In agreement with previous work, pre-monsoon aerosol deposition is dominated by dust originating from western sources and less frequently by transport from southerly air mass sources as demonstrated by evidence of one of the strongest recorded pre-monsoon events emanating from the Bay of Bengal, Cyclone Fani. Elevated concentrations of human-sourced metals (e.g., Pb, Bi, As) are found in surface snow and stream chemistry collected in the Khumbu region. As the most comprehensive case study of environmental chemistry in the Khumbu region, this research offers sufficient evidence for increased monitoring in this watershed and surrounding areas.

text:
यह रिपोर्ट स्ट्रैटोस्फियर में बहने वाली हवा की धारा QBO (Quasi-Biennial Oscillation) के नवंबर 2025 में असामान्य रूप से जल्दी पलटने की बात करती है — जबकि यह बदलाव सामान्यतः जनवरी-फरवरी में होता है। NOAA के जोनल विंड डेटा और मौसम विशेषज्ञों के हवाले से बताया गया है कि यह किसी स्थानीय घटना के बजाय पूरे ग्लोबल मौसम तंत्र में आई एक बड़ी गड़बड़ी है, जिसे पश्चिमी प्रशांत और हिंद महासागर के रिकॉर्ड गर्म तापमान तथा नवंबर 2025-फरवरी 2026 की ला नीना से जोड़ा गया है।
मुख्य बिंदु:

QBO क्या है और असर क्यों पड़ेगा: धरती से 20-30 किमी ऊपर चलने वाली यह हवा सामान्यतः हर ~2 साल में दिशा बदलती है; 2025 का बदलाव सामान्य से 2-3 महीने पहले हुआ, जिससे तूफान अनियमित होंगे और नमी असामान्य जगहों पर गिरेगी।
भारत पर मौसमी असर (2025-26): तमिलनाडु, आंध्र प्रदेश, केरल, कर्नाटक, पुडुचेरी में सामान्य से ज्यादा उत्तर-पूर्वी मॉनसून बारिश और बंगाल की खाड़ी में शक्तिशाली चक्रवात; अनियमित सर्दी (तेज ठंड के बाद अचानक गर्मी, घना कोहरा, हिमालय में ज्यादा बर्फबारी-हिमस्खलन का खतरा); मध्य भारत में रिकॉर्ड तोड़ गर्मी; और 2026 के दक्षिण-पश्चिम मॉनसून में देरी व असमान बंटवारा, जहां एक जिले में बाढ़ तो पड़ोसी जिले में सूखा।
दुनिया पर असर: यूरोप में ठंडी सर्दी के बाद अचानक बाढ़, कैलिफोर्निया में एटमॉस्फेरिक रिवर से भारी बारिश-बाढ़ का खतरा, ऑस्ट्रेलिया में बाढ़ या सूखा, और सऊदी अरब में अनियमित मौसम — इन देशों की जीडीपी में 1-2% तक गिरावट की आशंका।
मानव व आर्थिक असर: लू, बाढ़ और ठंड से स्वास्थ्य जोखिम; भारतीय कृषि पर 10-20% असर और जीडीपी में 0.5-1% तक गिरावट की संभावना, साथ ही रबी गेहूं, बागवानी फसलों और खरीफ धान-मक्का-सोयाबीन पर खतरा।
विशेषज्ञों की राय: IISER के प्रो. पंकज कुमार का कहना है कि स्थानीय बारिश भी असल में ग्लोबल मौसमी पैटर्न से जुड़ी होती है; पूर्व IIT रुड़की शोधकर्ता व ग्लेशियोलॉजिस्ट डॉ. प्रवीण कुमार सिंह भारत में बार-बार आने वाले “कंपाउंड एक्सट्रीम वेदर” — फ्लैश फ्लड, ग्लेशियर झील फटने का खतरा, और घटती लेकिन ज्यादा अनियमित औसत बारिश — की ओर इशारा करते हैं।
लेख यह भी बताता है कि QBO का टूटना हाल की ज्वालामुखी व भूकंप गतिविधियों से सीधे तकनीकी रूप से नहीं जुड़ा है, हालांकि दोनों को एक ही व्यापक जलवायु परिवर्तन के दौर से जोड़ा गया है।

title: रिवर्स गियर में हवा, Ice Age जैसा खतरा… भारत से लेकर यूरोप तक मौसम के सितम के पीछे का साइंस
text:
Summary (English)
The article reports that the stratospheric wind band known as the Quasi-Biennial Oscillation (QBO), which circulates roughly 20-30 km above the surface and normally reverses direction every 28-30 months (typically around January-February), reversed unusually early in November 2025. Citing NOAA zonal wind data and outside meteorologists, the piece frames this as a disruption to the broader climate system rather than an isolated event, tying it to record-warm sea-surface temperatures in the western Pacific and Indian Ocean and to the concurrent La Niña (November 2025-February 2026).
Key points covered:

What QBO is and why it matters: an upper-atmosphere wind engine that normally flips direction every ~2 years; its 2025 reversal came 2-3 months early per NOAA data, which the article links to storm irregularity and moisture falling in atypical locations.
India, season by season (2025-26): heavier-than-normal northeast monsoon rain over Tamil Nadu/Andhra Pradesh/Kerala/Karnataka/Puducherry and stronger Bay of Bengal cyclones; an erratic winter (sharper cold spells alternating with sudden warm swings, prolonged fog in the north, heavier Himalayan snow/avalanche risk); a record-hot summer forecast for central India; and a delayed, uneven 2026 southwest monsoon with clustering of flood and drought within the same states.
Elsewhere: colder winters followed by flooding in Europe, atmospheric-river flooding risk in California, flood-or-drought extremes in Australia, and disrupted conditions in Saudi Arabia — with an estimated 1-2% GDP hit cited for these economies.
Human and economic impacts: health risks from heat, flooding, and cold; an estimated 10-20% hit to Indian agriculture and a possible 0.5-1% drag on GDP growth, alongside crop-specific risk to rabi wheat, horticulture, and kharif rice/maize/soy.
Expert commentary: quotes IISER earth-and-environment scientist Prof. Pankaj Kumar on rainfall events reflecting global rather than purely local patterns, and former IIT Roorkee researcher/glaciologist Dr. Praveen Kumar Singh on India’s shift toward recurring “compound extreme weather,” including flash floods, glacial lake outburst risk, and declining but more erratic average rainfall.
Notes the QBO disruption is not itself linked mechanistically to the recent spate of volcanic and seismic activity mentioned in the article’s framing, though both are attributed to the same broader era of climate change.

title: Chamoli Disaster: क्या मौसम की वजह से हो सकता है चमोली जैसा हादसा? IIT’s की स्टडी
text:
यह फोटो-फीचर 7 फरवरी 2021 को उत्तराखंड के चमोली जिले में हुए रॉक-आइस एवलांच और उसके बाद आई फ्लैश फ्लड (जिसमें ~200 लोगों की जान गई) की घटना पर IIT रुड़की के सेंटर ऑफ एक्सीलेंस इन डिजास्टर मिटिगेशन एंड मैनेजमेंट और IIT दिल्ली के सेंटर फॉर एटमॉस्फेरिक साइंसेज के वैज्ञानिकों (प्रवीण कुमार सिंह, पीयूष श्रीवास्तव, प्रभाकर नामदेव) के अध्ययन पर आधारित है, जो जर्नल Atmosphere में प्रकाशित हुआ।
मुख्य बिंदु:

मौसम में अचानक बदलाव: घटना से तीन दिन पहले रोंटी पीक और आसपास के हिमालयी क्षेत्र में हवा व सतह का तापमान तेजी से गिरा; 4 फरवरी को बारिश हुई; घटना से 48 घंटे पहले तापमान औसत से 8.5°C नीचे और ऊंचाई की हवाएं सामान्य से 13°C ठंडी दर्ज हुईं — यह विश्लेषण ECMWF ERA5 डेटासेट पर आधारित है।
क्षेत्रीय पैटर्न: यह ठंडक, बारिश और उसके बाद की गर्मी स्थानीय नहीं बल्कि हिमालय के बड़े ऊंचाई वाले क्षेत्र में दर्ज हुई, जो बताता है कि व्यापक मौसमी पैटर्न ने भूस्खलन को बढ़ावा दिया।
भूगर्भीय क्रम (पूर्व अध्ययनों से): रोंटी पीक (6,063 मीटर) पर करीब आधा किमी चौड़ा पत्थर, जिस पर ~80 मीटर बर्फ जमी थी, 2016 से ही हिलना शुरू हो गया था; 7 फरवरी 2021 को यह टूटकर 5,500 मीटर नीचे रोंटी गैड में गिरा, जिससे दो झटके महसूस हुए और मलबा 205-216 किमी/घंटा की रफ्तार से बहा।
असर: ऋषिगंगा (13.2 मेगावॉट) और तपोवन (530 मेगावॉट) हाइड्रोपावर परियोजनाएं तबाह हुईं; गंगा का पानी 900 किमी दूर कानपुर तक 8 दिन तक गंदा रहा।
निष्कर्ष: वैज्ञानिकों के अनुसार पहले बताए गए कारणों (ऊंचाई से गिरा पत्थर-बर्फ, पत्थर-बर्फ अनुपात, हाइड्रोपावर स्टेशन की मौजूदगी) के साथ अब मौसमी बदलाव को भी इस आपदा का एक प्रमुख कारक माना जाना चाहिए।

This photo feature covers a joint study by IIT Roorkee’s Centre of Excellence in Disaster Mitigation and Management and IIT Delhi’s Centre for Atmospheric Sciences — researchers Praveen Kumar Singh, Piyush Srivastava, and Prabhakar Namdev — published in the journal Atmosphere, examining the weather conditions preceding the 7 February 2021 Chamoli rock-ice avalanche and flash flood in Uttarakhand, which killed around 200 people.
Key points:

Sudden weather shift: in the three days before the event, air and surface temperatures around Ronti Peak and the surrounding high-Himalayan area dropped sharply; rainfall occurred on 4 February; 48 hours before the 7 February event, temperatures were roughly 8.5°C below average and upper-elevation winds were about 13°C colder than normal, based on analysis of the ECMWF ERA5 dataset.
Regional, not local, pattern: the cooling, rain, and subsequent warming were recorded across a wide high-elevation stretch of the Himalaya rather than being a purely local event, suggesting a broader weather pattern contributed to triggering the slide.
Geological sequence (from earlier studies cited): a roughly half-kilometre-wide rock mass on the 6,063 m Ronti Peak, carrying about 80 m of ice, had been destabilizing since 2016; it broke away on 7 February 2021, fell roughly 5,500 m into the Ronti Gad stream (registering two seismic signals), and the resulting debris flow moved at an estimated 205-216 km/h.
Impact: the Rishiganga (13.2 MW) and Tapovan (530 MW) hydropower projects were destroyed, and Ganga river water remained turbid as far as Kanpur, roughly 900 km downstream, for eight days.
Takeaway: alongside previously cited causes — the falling rock-ice mass, the rock-to-ice ratio that drove glacier melt and breakup, and the unfortunate siting of hydropower infrastructure — the researchers argue the preceding weather anomaly should now be recognized as a major contributing factor.

title: Chamoli Disaster: क्या मौसम की वजह से हो सकता है चमोली जैसा हादसा? IIT’s की स्टडी
section: प्रवीण कुमार सिंह के बयान (Statements by Praveen Kumar Singh)
text:
प्रवीण कुमार सिंह के बयान (Statements by Praveen Kumar Singh)
Hindi: IIT रुड़की के शोधकर्ता प्रवीण कुमार सिंह ने aajtak.in से खास बातचीत में बताया कि चमोली रॉक-आइस एवलांच से तीन दिन पहले ही रोंटी पीक के ऊपर और आसपास के इलाके में मौसम तेजी से बदलने लगा था — हवा और सतह, दोनों का तापमान तेजी से गिरा और 4 फरवरी को बारिश हुई। उन्होंने बताया कि घटना से ठीक 48 घंटे पहले पीक के ऊपर का वायुमंडलीय और सतही तापमान औसत से 8.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस नीचे चला गया था, जबकि पहले के दिनों में स्थिति सामान्य थी।
आगे उन्होंने कहा कि उनकी स्टडी में यह सामने आया कि एवलांच से पहले अचानक मौसम का ठंडा होना, तेज बारिश और उत्तर-पश्चिम दिशा से बहने वाली तेज हवाएं — इन सबने मिलकर इस घटना को बढ़ावा दिया। उनके मुताबिक मौसम में यह बदलाव चमोली हादसे की एक प्रमुख वजह था, जिस पर पहले किसी का ध्यान नहीं गया था। यह अध्ययन प्रवीण कुमार सिंह, पीयूष श्रीवास्तव और प्रभाकर नामदेव ने मिलकर किया और जर्नल Atmosphere में प्रकाशित हुआ।
English: In comments to aajtak.in, IIT Roorkee researcher Praveen Kumar Singh explained that weather around Ronti Peak and the surrounding area began shifting rapidly in the three days before the rock-ice avalanche, with both air and surface temperatures dropping sharply and rain falling on 4 February. He noted that exactly 48 hours before the 7 February event, atmospheric and surface temperatures above the peak had fallen 8.5°C below average, a sharp break from the otherwise normal conditions in the preceding days.
He went on to say that the study found the sudden cooling, heavy rainfall, and strong northwesterly winds in the run-up to the avalanche together helped trigger the event, describing this weather shift as a major, previously overlooked factor behind the Chamoli disaster. The study was carried out jointly by Praveen Kumar Singh, Piyush Srivastava, and Prabhakar Namdev, and was published in the journal Atmosphere.

text:
The 2019 Everest Expedition, led by the National Geographic Society in partnership with Nepal’s Tribhuvan University and supported by Rolex, launched the Perpetual Planet Everest Expedition, was one of the most comprehensive scientific expeditions ever conducted on Mount Everest. From April to June 2019, a multidisciplinary team of scientists, climbers, and explorers carried out research to better understand the impacts of climate change on the Himalayan environment. The expedition installed the world’s highest operating weather stations, collected ice-core and water samples, mapped glaciers, and studied ecosystems at extreme elevations. title: Praveen Kumar Singh
text:
Hey, I’m glad you’re here

Thanks for stopping by!
I’m a Postdoctoral Research Scientist at the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique (LMD) – IPSL, where I study how atmospheric pollutants interact with meteorology and climate across South and Southeast Asia. But if you’d told the 2011 version of me - freshly graduated in electronics and communication engineering, about to spend a year working on telecom systems in Eastern India - that I’d eventually be chasing black carbon up in the Himalayas, I don’t think he’d have believed you.
Most of my work orbits one question: what happens when short-lived climate pollutants — black carbon especially — meet the world’s most climate-sensitive mountain system? I trace how these particles travel, deposit, and reshape radiative forcing across the Hindu Kush Himalaya, and what that means for glacier melt, snow albedo, and the water resources millions of people downstream depend on.

title: Praveen Kumar Singh
text:
About me


Electronics engineer turned atmospheric scientist, still most at home somewhere between a supercomputer cluster and a glacier. Drawn to the places where air, ice, and people meet - and to understanding the systems that connect them.
My path here wasn’t a straight line. I started in electronics and communication engineering, worked briefly as a telecom engineer, and then followed a growing pull toward environmental science - first through a master’s from Central University of Rajasthan and later through a Ph.D. at IIT Roorkee.


Ph.D. in Atmospheric Science ∙ Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee ∙ 2024


M.Sc. in Environmental Science ∙ Central University of Rajasthan ∙ 2016


B.Tech. in Electronics & Communication Engineering ∙ Gautam Buddh Technical University ∙ 2011


How I got here
My journey into atmospheric and cryosphere science began slowly, then all at once. A telecom job that paid the bills but left me curious about a bigger question: what is pollution actually doing to the air, water, and ice we depend on? So, I returned to university to pursue environmental science, where I ended up measuring methane emissions across the semi-arid land uses of Rajasthan. Unglamorous, field-heavy work, and I loved it.


That fieldwork took me to the Himalayas. At IIT Roorkee and subsequently ICIMOD in Kathmandu, I worked on in-situ measurements, atmospheric remote sensing, and glacier energy and mass balance modeling. Then came the expedition that remains pivotal to most of my stories: in 2019, I joined National Geographic’s Perpetual Planet Everest Expedition, where I measured light-absorbing pollutants in snow at Everest Base Camp. That event fueled my curiosity about how air pollution affects mountain landscapes and water resources.
During my Ph.D. at IIT Roorkee, I studied black carbon in the Hindu Kush Himalaya, combining satellite data with regional climate and general circulation models. Eventually, the problems I was exploring began to overlap with policy, so I pursued a diploma in Environmental Law and Policy.


Post Graduate Diploma in Environmental Law and Policy ∙ National Law University Delhi ∙ 2022


Before moving to Palaiseau, I spent nearly two years as a Senior Program Associate - Air Quality at WRI India, where I engaged directly with the Gorakhpur city administration to formulate pollution reduction strategies across multiple sectors, including transportation, waste, industry, and household energy, and assisted in translating scientific analyses into implementable policies for officials.



What I’m working on now
At LMD, I am investigating the interplay between atmospheric contaminants, meteorological conditions, and climate in South and Southeast Asia – research that builds on years of tracking black carbon throughout the Hindu Kush Himalaya. My latest publications encompass aerosol composition and movement in the Central Himalaya, fluctuations in black carbon across the area, and partnerships examining glacier ice loss patterns and winter meteorological conditions at the summit of Everest. I am captivated by the initial inquiry that sparked my exploration: how do these unseen particles alter mountain climates, and what implications does this have for downstream populations?

title: Fire and Ice: Soot Darkens Himalayan Glaciers
text:
This Dialogue Earth piece by Rishika Pardikar reports on how forest fires and crop-residue burning in the Terai Arc Landscape and Himalayan foothills — combined with emissions from coal power, transport, and brick kilns — deposit black carbon (soot) on Himalayan glaciers, disrupting the light-reflecting (albedo) properties that have historically preserved the ice.
Key points:

Fire-prone Terai region: citing a Forest Survey of India technical study, the article notes roughly 37.54% of Uttar Pradesh’s forest cover and 32.75% of Uttarakhand’s forest cover (within the Terai belt) is extremely-to-moderately fire-prone; Pilibhit Tiger Reserve deputy director Naveen Khandelwal described dry-season grassland fires and crop-residue burning near farms as contributing causes.
How black carbon accelerates melt: black carbon settling on glacier surfaces darkens them, increasing light and heat absorption and driving snow/ice melt; suspended black carbon in the atmosphere also warms surrounding air, compounding melt and affecting monsoon patterns.
Seasonal drivers: ICIMOD senior aerosol scientist Siva Praveen Puppala said roughly 30-40% of black carbon deposition in the Himalayan region during April-May comes from forest fires; Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology scientist P.S. Negi linked high black carbon concentrations to both summer (April-May) forest fires and winter (October-November) crop burning, with some crop burning also occurring in summer.
Compounding effect: Puppala explained that as black carbon from current fires melts a glacier’s top layer, it exposes older black carbon deposits buried in lower layers, further darkening the surface and accelerating melt.
Field evidence: a 2019 paper co-authored by Negi found black carbon concentration near Gangotri glacier’s Chirbasa site peaked in May and was lowest in August, linked to agricultural burning in western India and Himalayan-slope forest fires; separate ICIMOD work on Nepal’s Yala glacier attributed about 23% of 2016-17 annual black carbon concentration to forest fires and agricultural burning.
Data caveats: fire-count analysis for 2015-2019 (based on VIIRS satellite data, which observes Earth’s surface only twice daily and generally can’t detect fires smaller than about one square kilometre) shows April and October as peak fire months, though the article notes true fire extent — especially small-plot crop burning common on India’s 2-3 acre farms — is likely undercounted.
Outlook: because black carbon is a short-lived climate pollutant (lasting weeks in the atmosphere, unlike CO2’s centuries), the article frames fire control and crop-residue alternatives as offering faster visible results than carbon dioxide mitigation; Dudhwa Tiger Reserve ranger Pradeep Varma described ongoing but under-resourced efforts like fire lines to limit spread during the high-risk April-May window.

title: Mt. Everest Ice Loss: दुनिया के सबसे ऊंचे पहाड़ से 32 साल में इतना ग्लेशियर पिघला जितना 2000 साल में बनता
text:
यह फोटो-फीचर 2019 में माउंट एवरेस्ट के साउथ कोल ग्लेशियर (South Col Glacier, ~8,000 मीटर ऊंचाई) पर गई एक अंतरराष्ट्रीय वैज्ञानिक टीम के अध्ययन पर आधारित है, जो जर्नल npj Climate and Atmospheric Science में प्रकाशित हुआ। इस टीम में IIT रुड़की के सेंटर ऑफ एक्सीलेंस इन डिजास्टर मिटिगेशन एंड मैनेजमेंट के पीएचडी स्कॉलर और काठमांडू स्थित ICIMOD (International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development) के सदस्य प्रवीण कुमार सिंह भी शामिल थे।
मुख्य बिंदु:

पिघलने की दर: साउथ कोल ग्लेशियर सामान्य से करीब 80 गुना तेजी से पिघल रहा है। 1990 से अब तक इतनी बर्फ पिघल चुकी है जितनी जमने में सामान्य परिस्थितियों में करीब 2,000 साल लगते; हर साल ग्लेशियर उतनी बर्फ खो रहा है जितनी बनने में एक दशक लगता।
पद्धति: वैज्ञानिकों ने दो ऊंचाई पर (27,600 फीट और 26,200 फीट) मौसम-निगरानी स्टेशन लगाए और ग्लेशियर से 10 मीटर गहरी ड्रिलिंग कर बर्फ के नमूने लिए, फिर कंप्यूटर सिमुलेशन से पिघलने-जमने की प्रक्रिया का विश्लेषण किया। नतीजा — पिछले 25 वर्षों में ग्लेशियर ने करीब 180 फीट बर्फ खोई है।
वजह: तेज हवाएं और नमी में बदलाव भी योगदान देते हैं, लेकिन मानव-प्रेरित जलवायु परिवर्तन सबसे बड़ा कारक है — 1950 के दशक से ग्लेशियर पतला होना शुरू हुआ और 1990 के बाद यह प्रक्रिया काफी तेज हो गई, क्योंकि पिघली बर्फ की परत सूरज की सीधी रोशनी के संपर्क में आने लगी।
व्यापक हिमालयी संदर्भ: लेख में University of Leeds (जर्नल Nature, 20 दिसंबर प्रकाशित) के एक अलग अध्ययन का हवाला दिया गया है, जिसमें 14,798 हिमालयी ग्लेशियरों का विश्लेषण कर पाया गया कि वे छोटे हिमयुग (Little Ice Age) के बाद अपना ~40% क्षेत्र (28,000 वर्ग किमी से घटकर 19,600 वर्ग किमी) और 390-590 घन किमी बर्फ खो चुके हैं, जिससे वैश्विक समुद्र-स्तर में 0.92-1.38 मिमी की वृद्धि हुई; पिघलने की गति पिछले दशकों में पिछली सदियों की तुलना में ~10 गुना बढ़ी है।
असर: हिमालय के ग्लेशियरों से निकलने वाली नदियां (गंगा, सिंधु, ब्रह्मपुत्र सहित) लगभग 100 करोड़ लोगों को पीने व सिंचाई का पानी देती हैं; पिघलने की तेज़ रफ्तार से भारत, नेपाल, चीन, बांग्लादेश, भूटान, पाकिस्तान जैसे देशों में भविष्य में पानी की गंभीर किल्लत का खतरा है।

title: Mt. Everest Ice Loss: दुनिया के सबसे ऊंचे पहाड़ से 32 साल में इतना ग्लेशियर पिघला जितना 2000 साल में बनता
text:
Summary (English)
This photo feature covers a 2019 international scientific expedition to Mount Everest’s South Col Glacier (roughly 8,000 m elevation), published in the journal npj Climate and Atmospheric Science. The team included Praveen Kumar Singh, a PhD scholar at IIT Roorkee’s Centre of Excellence in Disaster Mitigation and Management and a member of ICIMOD (International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development) in Kathmandu.
Key points:

Rate of melt: the South Col Glacier is thinning roughly 80 times faster than normal. Since 1990, it has lost ice that took about 2,000 years to accumulate, and it is now losing, in a single year, roughly as much ice as would normally take a decade to form.
Methodology: the team installed two weather-monitoring stations (at 27,600 ft and 26,200 ft) and drilled a 10-metre ice core from the glacier, then ran computer simulations of melt and accumulation — finding the glacier has lost about 180 feet of ice over the past 25 years.
Cause: strong winds and shifting humidity play a role, but human-driven climate change is described as the dominant factor — the glacier began thinning in the 1950s, with the rate accelerating sharply after 1990 as the melting snow layer exposed the glacier’s surface directly to sunlight.
Wider Himalayan context: the article also cites a separate University of Leeds study (published in Nature on 20 December) that analyzed 14,798 Himalayan glaciers since the Little Ice Age and found they have lost about 40% of their area (from 28,000 km² to 19,600 km²) and 390-590 km³ of ice, contributing 0.92-1.38 mm to global sea-level rise, with melt rates roughly 10 times faster in recent decades than in prior centuries. The study’s lead author, Jonathan Carrivick, is quoted attributing this acceleration to human-driven climate change and global warming.
Impact: rivers fed by Himalayan glaciers — including the Ganga, Indus, and Brahmaputra — supply drinking and irrigation water to roughly a billion people; at current melt rates, countries including India, Nepal, China, Bangladesh, Bhutan, and Pakistan face a growing risk of severe future water scarcity.

प्रवीण कुमार सिंह के बयान (Statements by Praveen Kumar Singh)
Statement below is from the author, Dr. Praveen Kumar Singh.
Hindi: प्रवीण कुमार सिंह ने aajtak.in से बातचीत में बताया कि टीम ने एवरेस्ट पर दो मौसम स्टेशन तैनात किए, ताकि ग्लेशियर के केंद्र से बर्फ के नमूने जमा किए जा सकें। जांच में पता चला कि साउथ कोल ग्लेशियर सामान्य से करीब 80 गुना तेज़ी से पिघल रहा है।
उन्होंने बताया कि टीम यह जानना चाहती थी कि क्या एवरेस्ट जैसी ऊंचाई पर मौजूद ग्लेशियरों पर भी इंसानी गतिविधियों और जलवायु परिवर्तन का असर पड़ता है — और जवाब हां में मिला, कम से कम 1990 के बाद से स्थितियां लगातार बिगड़ती जा रही हैं। उन्होंने यह भी बताया कि साउथ कोल ग्लेशियर 1950 के दशक से ही पतला होना शुरू हो गया था, और 1990 के दशक तक आते-आते पिघलने की दर काफी बढ़ गई।
English: In comments to aajtak.in, Praveen Kumar Singh explained that the team deployed two weather stations on Everest to collect ice-core samples from the glacier’s centre, and that this revealed the South Col Glacier is thinning roughly 80 times faster than normal.

title: बर्फ पिघलेगी… बारिश बढ़ेगी…गंगा का पानी का फ्लो 50% बढे़गा… अधिक आपदाएं आएंगी, IIT रुड़की के वैज्ञानिकों की स्टडी
text:
यह रिपोर्ट IIT रुड़की के शोधकर्ता डॉ. प्रवीण कुमार सिंह और राजीव रंजन के एक अध्ययन पर आधारित है, जिसमें गंगा नदी के हिंदू कुश हिमालय स्थित ऊपरी क्षेत्र (देवप्रयाग तक) पर जलवायु परिवर्तन के असर का आकलन किया गया है। अध्ययन में SPHY (Spatial Processes in Hydrology) हाइड्रोलॉजिकल मॉडल और CMIP6 के दो जलवायु परिदृश्यों (SSP2-4.5 और SSP5-8.5) का उपयोग कर देवप्रयाग के ऐतिहासिक प्रवाह आंकड़ों से मॉडल को सत्यापित किया गया।
मुख्य बिंदु:

वर्तमान स्थिति (1985-2014): देवप्रयाग में औसत कुल प्रवाह ~792 क्यूबिक मीटर/सेकंड रहा है, जिसमें बारिश का योगदान 63.3% (509.5 m³/s), बर्फ पिघलने का 14.9% (117.5 m³/s), ग्लेशियर पिघलने का 10.8% (86.1 m³/s) और भूजल (बेसफ्लो) का 10% (78.9 m³/s) है।
भविष्य का अनुमान (2076-2100): SSP5-8.5 जैसे उच्च-उत्सर्जन परिदृश्य में सदी के अंत तक तापमान और वर्षा में उल्लेखनीय वृद्धि होगी। मॉडल के अनुसार कुल नदी प्रवाह ~50% तक बढ़ सकता है, जिसका मुख्य कारण बढ़ी हुई बारिश होगी, इसके बाद ग्लेशियर पिघलना और भूजल।
बर्फ पिघलने में गिरावट: 2090 तक सीधे बर्फ पिघलने से मिलने वाला पानी ~57% तक घट सकता है, क्योंकि बढ़ता तापमान बर्फ भंडार को तेजी से घटा देगा।
कुल आपूर्ति फिर भी बनी रहेगी: भले ही बर्फ का योगदान घटे, बारिश और ग्लेशियर पिघलने से पानी की कुल आपूर्ति बनी रहने का अनुमान है — लेकिन यह प्रवाह अधिक मौसमी (seasonal) और बाढ़-प्रवण हो सकता है।
महत्व: अध्ययन सिंचाई, पेयजल और आपदा प्रबंधन नीति के लिए महत्वपूर्ण माना गया है, विशेषकर बाढ़, सूखे और पानी की कमी जैसी समस्याओं की भविष्य की योजना बनाने में।

title: बर्फ पिघलेगी… बारिश बढ़ेगी…गंगा का पानी का फ्लो 50% बढे़गा… अधिक आपदाएं आएंगी, IIT रुड़की के वैज्ञानिकों की स्टडी
text:
Summary (English)
The article reports on an IIT Roorkee hydrological study — led by researchers Dr. Praveen Kumar Singh and Rajiv Ranjan — assessing how climate change will affect water flow and balance in the Upper Ganga sub-basin of the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH), up to the Devprayag gauge point. The team used the SPHY (Spatial Processes in Hydrology) model together with two CMIP6 climate scenarios (SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5), calibrated and validated against historical discharge records at Devprayag.
Key findings:

Baseline (1985-2014): average total discharge at Devprayag was about 792 m³/s, with rainfall contributing 63.3% (509.5 m³/s), snowmelt 14.9% (117.5 m³/s), glacier melt 10.8% (86.1 m³/s), and baseflow/groundwater 10% (78.9 m³/s).
Projected changes (2076-2100): under the higher-emissions SSP5-8.5 pathway especially, both temperature and precipitation are projected to rise markedly by century’s end. Total river flow could increase by roughly 50%, driven mainly by rainfall runoff, followed by glacier melt and baseflow.
Declining snowmelt: the direct snowmelt contribution could fall by about 57% by 2090 as rising temperatures deplete the region’s snow reserves faster.
No overall water shortage projected: even with a shrinking snowmelt share, rainfall and glacier melt are expected to keep total water supply from falling — though flow is likely to become more seasonal and flood-prone.
Why it matters: the researchers frame the study as a basis for water-resource planning, irrigation, drinking-water security, and disaster (flood/drought) management policy across the Ganga basin and the wider Himalayan region.

शोधकर्ताओं के बयान (Statements by the Researchers)
Statement below from Dr. Praveen Kumar Singh is from the author.
डॉ. प्रवीण कुमार सिंह (Dr. Praveen Kumar Singh) — Hindi: IIT रुड़की के शोधकर्ता डॉ. प्रवीण कुमार सिंह ने बताया कि यह अध्ययन गंगा नदी के ऊपरी क्षेत्र में जलवायु परिवर्तन के प्रभाव को समझने के लिए किया गया, खासतौर पर यह देखने के लिए कि भविष्य में नदी का पानी, बर्फ का पिघलना, ग्लेशियर का पानी और भूजल कैसे बदल सकता है। उन्होंने बताया कि इसके लिए उन्होंने SPHY (Spatial Processes in Hydrology) नामक हाइड्रोलॉजिकल मॉडल और CMIP6 के दो जलवायु परिदृश्यों — SSP2-4.5 और SSP5-8.5 — का उपयोग किया, जो भविष्य में तापमान और वर्षा में होने वाले बदलावों का अनुमान लगाते हैं। मॉडल को देवप्रयाग में दर्ज नदी-प्रवाह के आंकड़ों से जांचा और सत्यापित किया गया।
Dr. Praveen Kumar Singh — English: IIT Roorkee researcher Dr. Praveen Kumar Singh explained that the study was designed to understand the impact of climate change on the Upper Ganga sub-basin, specifically examining how river discharge, snowmelt, glacier melt, and groundwater contributions might change in the future. He said the team used a hydrological model called SPHY (Spatial Processes in Hydrology) together with two CMIP6 climate scenarios — SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 — which project future changes in temperature and precipitation. The model was calibrated and validated against observed river-discharge data at Devprayag.
राजीव रंजन (Rajiv Ranjan) — Hindi: इस अध्ययन में शामिल शोधकर्ता राजीव रंजन ने कहा कि हिमालय क्षेत्र की नदियां, जैसे गंगा, लाखों लोगों के लिए जीवन रेखा हैं, जो खेती, पेयजल और उद्योगों के लिए पानी प्रदान करती हैं। उन्होंने कहा कि जलवायु परिवर्तन के कारण इन नदियों का प्रवाह बदल रहा है, और यह अध्ययन यह समझने में मदद करता है कि भविष्य में पानी की उपलब्धता कैसी होगी — जिससे सरकार और नीति-निर्माताओं को बाढ़, सूखे और जल-संकट जैसी चुनौतियों की योजना बनाने में मदद मिलेगी।
Rajiv Ranjan — English: Study co-researcher Rajiv Ranjan said Himalayan rivers such as the Ganga are a lifeline for millions of people, supplying water for agriculture, drinking, and industry. He noted that climate change is altering the flow of these rivers, and that the study helps in understanding how future water availability will look — information he said would help governments and policymakers plan for challenges like floods, droughts, and water scarcity.

title: Methane Emission and Its Variability in Different Land-uses of Semi-arid Region, Rajasthan
text: For the first time an attempt was made to quantify the methane fluxes in the different land-uses of the semi-arid region in India. Measurement of methane fluxes was carried out using static chamber in a highly saline wetland – Sambhar Lake, an urban lake – Mansagar Lake, a small reservoir – Kanota Dam and a landfill site in Jaipur district of Rajasthan, India. The results showed that semi-arid region has a significant impact on the methane budget. The parameters for water and soil were also studied and a positive correlation of soil organic matter and total organic carbon with methane fluxes were obtained. In the presence of high sulphate, methane production was observed at Kanota Dam which may be due to the symbiotic relationship between methanogens and sulphur reducing bacteria. The study revealed that the role of the semi-arid region is important for global methane budgeting and Sambhar Lake may play a significant role in methane budget with suitable conservation measures.

The results showed that semi-arid region has a significant impact on the methane budget. The parameters for water and soil were also studied and a positive correlation of soil organic matter and total organic carbon with methane fluxes were obtained. In the presence of high sulphate, methane production was observed at Kanota Dam which may be due to the symbiotic relationship between methanogens and sulphur reducing bacteria. The study revealed that the role of the semi-arid region is important for global methane budgeting and Sambhar Lake may play a significant role in methane budget with suitable conservation measures.

title: Black carbon concentration in the central Himalayas: Impact on glacier melt and potential source contribution
text: This study discusses year-long (October 2016–September 2017) observations of atmospheric black carbon (BC) mass concentration, its source and sector contributions using a chemical transport model at a high-altitude (28°12′49.21″N, 85°36′33.77″E, 4900 masl) site located near the Yala Glacier in the central Himalayas, Nepal. During a field campaign, fresh snow samples were collected from the surface of the Yala Glacier in May 2017, which were analysed for BC and water-insoluble organic carbon mass concentration in order to estimate the scavenging ratio and surface albedo reduction. The maximum BC mass concentration in the ambient atmosphere (0.73 μg m−3) was recorded in the pre-monsoon season. The BC and water-insoluble organic carbon analysed from the snow samples were in the range of 96–542 ng g−1 and 152–827 ng g−1, respectively. The source apportionment study using the absorption Ångström exponent from in situ observations indicated approximately 44% contribution of BC from biomass-burning sources and the remainder from fossil-fuel sources during the entire study period. The source contribution study, using model data sets, indicated ∼14% contribution of BC from open-burning and ∼77% from anthropogenic sources during the study period. Our analysis of regional contributions of BC indicated that the highest contribution was from both Nepal and India combined, followed by China, while the rest was distributed among the nearby countries. The surface snow albedo reduction, estimated by an online model – Snow, Ice, and Aerosol Radiation – was in the range of 0.8–3.8% during the pre-monsoon season. The glacier mass balance analysis suggested that BC contributed to approximately 39% of the total mass loss in the pre-monsoon season.

title: Mt. Everest’s highest glacier is a sentinel for accelerating ice loss
text: Mountain glacier systems are decreasing in volume worldwide yet relatively little is known about their upper reaches (>5000 m). Here we show, based on the world’s highest ice core and highest automatic weather stations, the significant and increasing role that melting and sublimation have on the mass loss of even Mt. Everest’s highest glacier (South Col Glacier, 8020 m). Estimated contemporary thinning rates approaching ~2 m a-1 water equivalent (w.e.) indicate several decades of accumulation may be lost on an annual basis now that glacier ice has been exposed. These results identify extreme sensitivity to glacier surface type for high altitude Himalayan ice masses and forewarn of rapidly emerging impacts as Mt. Everest’s highest glacier appears destined for rapid retreat.

title: Decadal Changes in Atmospheric Methane Emissions in the Eastern Himalayan Region: Source Apportionment and Impact Assessment
text: Methane (CH4), the second-largest greenhouse gas in terms of radiative forcing, is on the rise in the Eastern Himalayan region (EHR), as indicated by multiple datasets (CAMS ~ 0.087 Tg Yr-1, EDGAR v4.3.2 ~ 0.11 Tg Yr-1, and RCP8.5 ~ 0.16 Tg Yr-1). We found that the CH4 trend over the EHR is stronger than the global trend due to increased emissions from anthropogenic sources. From 1990 to 2016, CH4 emissions from anthropogenic activities and wetlands increased by 20% and 10% over the EHR. The land-use land-cover (LULC) change reveals a loss of ~ 0.42% of forest and an increase of 0.018% of urban built-up, 0.098% total wetland, and 0.033% of water-bodies coverage from 2001 to 2018. Future projections show a twofold (32.7 Tg CH4 Yr-1) increase in CH4 emissions by 2050 and up to a threefold (~ 48.2 Tg CH4 Yr-1) by the year 2100 from the base year level (14.6 Tg CH4 Yr-1) in 2000. Ambient concentrations of CH4 measured in Dibrugarh and the CAMS reanalysis data set from March 2014 to February 2015 show the maximum in December (~ 4485 and ~ 1981 ppb, respectively), while the minimum concentrations in July (~ 1155 ppb and ~ 976 ppb). The calculated global/EHR RF due to the CH4 for 2006–2100 is higher (0.0093 Wm-2 Yr-1/0.0095 Wm-2 Yr-1) than the historical (0.0038 Wm-2 Yr-1/0.0037 Wm-2 Yr-1) during 1851–2005. The resultant land surface temperature increase induced solely by CH4 is higher over the EHR (~ 0.0062 °C Yr-1) than the global (~ 0.0036 °C Yr-1).

title: Insights from the first winter weather observations near Mount Everest’s summit
text: The highest reaches of our planet experience some of the most extreme weather on Earth and hold very significant supplies of freshwater for communities downstream. However, we know very little of the meteorological detail about this high-altitude frontier. We address this here with new winter weather observations from the upper reaches of Mount Everest (2019–2021). We show that substantial sublimation rates are possible, with losses up to 2.5 mm day−1. Wind chill plunging to −83°C and frostbite possible in less than one minute also attest to the severe cold stress facing mountaineers attempting winter ascents of this most iconic peak.

title: Climate change impact assessment on the river discharge of the upper Ganga Subbasin
text: The HKH region has many glaciers, providing fresh water to a large population downstream. The hydrological system is susceptible to climate change, especially temperature and precipitation. The present study aims to investigate the impact of climate change on the discharge and water balance of the snow-dominated upper Ganga Basin. The study utilized CMIP6 scenarios SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 with SPHY to simulate future hydrological changes in the basin. We calibrated and validated the model for simulation by using observed discharge data at Devprayag. The historical period (1985–2014) calibrated at Devprayag showed rainfall, snow, glacier, baseflow, and total discharge of 509.5 m3/s, 117.5 m3/s, 86.1 m3/s, 78.9 m3/s, and 792.0 m3/s, respectively. Contribution to total flow was 63.3% (rain), 10.8% (glaciermelt), 14.9% (snowmelt), and 10.0% (baseflow). Total runoff increased, with rainfall runoff, contributing the most, followed by glaciermelt runoff and baseflow, while snowmelt decreased. By the end of 21st century, temperature and precipitation is anticipated to rise under SSP5-8.5. The model estimates substantially impacted the basin hydrology and water balance, with a 50% increase in total flow in the Far Future (2076–2100). The snowmelt contribution is estimated to decrease by 57% by 2090, but the water supply is not expected to desrease. The analysis showed that snowmelt runoff will be reduced through time, and river discharge will be highly impacted by climate change. This work will improve understanding of water availability, snowmelt, and glacier melt dynamics, which, along with climate change, lead to sustainable water resource management.
